definition:
The church is the people God has gathered to himself through Jesus Christ: every person, in every age and place, who has been joined to Christ by the Holy Spirit through faith, together with the visible congregations in which those people meet to hear God's word, pray, receive baptism and the Lord's Supper, care for one another, and bear witness to the world. It is not first a building, an institution, or a religious service, though it has all three. It is a people. From the call of Abraham onward, God's purpose in Scripture is never only to rescue scattered individuals but to form a community that belongs to him, lives under his rule, and shows the world what he is like. The Old Testament calls that people Israel; the New Testament announces that in Christ, Jews and Gentiles together have become “members of God's household” (Ephesians 2:19), and it describes them with a cluster of images: the body of Christ, the bride of Christ, the temple of the Spirit, the flock of the good shepherd, and the household of God. The Christian creeds confess the church as one, holy, catholic (that is, universal), and apostolic.

The Hebrew Bible has two main words for Israel as a gathered people. Qahal means an ‘assembly’ or ‘convocation’, people called together for a purpose, and it is used of Israel gathered at Sinai, which Deuteronomy calls “the day of the assembly” (Deuteronomy 9:10). ‘Edah, usually translated ‘congregation’, names Israel as a community, as in “the whole congregation of Israel” at the first Passover (Exodus 12:3). When Jewish scholars translated the Scriptures into Greek in the centuries before Christ (the Septuagint), they most often rendered qahal with ekklēsia and ‘edah with synagōgē. Ekklēsia was an ordinary Greek word for an assembly of citizens: Luke uses it for the rioting crowd in the theater at Ephesus (Acts 19:32) and for “a legal assembly” (Acts 19:39). When the early Christians chose ekklēsia for themselves, they were claiming to be the assembly of the God of Israel, not a private society. Preachers sometimes say ekklēsia means ‘the called-out ones’ because it is built from ek, ‘out’, and kaleō, ‘call’; that is an etymological fallacy, since no Greek speaker heard the word that way, and its meaning in use is simply ‘assembly’. The English word ‘church’ (like the Scots ‘kirk’ and the German Kirche) comes by a different route, from the Greek kyriakon, ‘belonging to the Lord’. The New Testament uses ekklēsia about 114 times, for a local congregation (1 Corinthians 1:2), for a house church (Romans 16:5), for the believers of a region (Acts 9:31), and for the whole people of Christ (Ephesians 1:22-23).
ot:
The story of the church begins long before Pentecost. After Babel, where humanity tried to make a name for itself and was scattered (Genesis 11:4), God called one man and promised, “I will make you into a great nation,” adding that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:2-3). From the start, then, God's people exist for the sake of others. The promise passes through Isaac and Jacob, whose sons become the tribes of Israel, and it is sealed in a covenant, a binding relationship God establishes by promise and oath. At Sinai God tells the people he has rescued from Egypt, “I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself” (Exodus 19:4), and then names their identity and calling: “you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations” and “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5-6). Deuteronomy insists that this choice rested on nothing in Israel: “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7). The people of God are a people of grace before they are a people of law.

The gathering at Sinai becomes the pattern for Israel's life. God tells Moses, “Gather the people before Me to hear My words” (Deuteronomy 4:10), and Israel is again and again called together as a qahal to hear the law, renew the covenant, and worship: at the dedication of Solomon's temple “the whole assembly of Israel stood there” (1 Kings 8:14), and after the exile Ezra read the law to the assembled people (Nehemiah 8). The heart of this people's life is God's presence among them. The promise “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:12) runs from the tabernacle through the temple and the prophets to the last page of the Bible. The assembly also had boundaries, some of which the New Testament overturns: Deuteronomy excluded eunuchs and Ammonites and Moabites from “the assembly of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 23:1-3), yet the book of Ruth tells how a Moabite woman became an ancestor of David, and Isaiah promised eunuchs and foreigners a place in God's house (Isaiah 56:3-7).

The history of Israel is also the history of a people who failed their calling. The prophets indicted kings, priests, and people for idolatry and injustice, and the exile to Assyria and Babylon seemed to end Israel's story. Yet the same prophets announced that God would keep a remnant (Isaiah 10:20-22) and would one day make “a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,” writing his law on their hearts so that “they will all know Me” (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Ezekiel pictured God himself searching for his scattered flock (Ezekiel 34:11-12), raising dry bones to life (Ezekiel 37), and making “an everlasting covenant” with a people among whom he would set his sanctuary forever (Ezekiel 37:26-27). Hosea, whose children were named ‘Not My People’ as a sign of judgment, heard God promise, “I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people’” (Hosea 2:23). And the prophets looked for the nations to join Israel: “all nations will stream to it” (Isaiah 2:2), to the mountain of the LORD's house. The Old Testament closes with a people waiting to be regathered, renewed by the Spirit, and enlarged to include the world.
nt:
Jesus began by calling twelve disciples, a number that deliberately echoes the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28), and he gathered around himself a renewed Israel of the poor, the sinners, and the outcasts. Only Matthew among the Gospels records Jesus using the word ekklēsia, twice. After Peter confesses him as the Christ, Jesus says, “on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18), and he gives the keys of the kingdom and the authority to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19). Later he entrusts the same binding and loosing to the gathered community in a case of unrepented sin: “tell it to the church” (Matthew 18:17), with the promise that “where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them” (Matthew 18:20). The church is Christ's own building, and he is present in it. In John, Jesus is the good shepherd who has “other sheep that are not of this fold,” so that “there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16), and he prays for all future believers “that all of them may be one” so “that the world may believe” (John 17:21). The unity of the church is part of its witness.

The church as a public community is born at Pentecost, when the Spirit promised by the prophets is poured out and about three thousand people are baptized. Luke's portrait is simple: “They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42), they shared their goods with the needy, and “the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved” (Acts 2:47). The rest of Acts tells how this community, first entirely Jewish, crossed boundaries it had not expected to cross: to Samaritans, to an Ethiopian official, to the Roman centurion Cornelius, and to Greeks in Antioch, where “the disciples were first called Christians” (Acts 11:26). The Jerusalem council of Acts 15 settled that Gentiles did not need to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong, a decision of the apostles and elders “with the whole church” (Acts 15:22).

Paul supplies the richest theology of the church. It is the body of Christ: “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27), a unity of many different members, “whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free” (1 Corinthians 12:13), each needing the others. In Ephesians and Colossians, Christ is the head of that body (Colossians 1:18), and the church is “His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:23). It is the temple of God: “you yourselves are God's temple” (1 Corinthians 3:16), a building rising on “the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone” and becoming “a dwelling place for God in His Spirit” (Ephesians 2:20-22). It is the bride, whom “Christ loved” and for whom he “gave Himself up” (Ephesians 5:25). Paul's great claim in Ephesians 2 is that Christ has “made the two one,” Jew and Gentile, tearing down “the dividing wall of hostility” to “create in Himself one new man out of the two” (Ephesians 2:14-15), so that through the church “the manifold wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms” (Ephesians 3:10). Paul applies to the church the language of Israel's promises, quoting Hosea (Romans 9:25-26), calling Gentile believers Abraham's seed (Galatians 3:29), and picturing them as wild olive branches grafted into Israel's tree, supported by a root they do not support (Romans 11:17-18). How the church relates to Israel after Christ is taken up in the study on Israel in God's purpose.

The later letters show the church settling into ordered life. It is “God's household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). Hebrews warns, “Let us not neglect meeting together” (Hebrews 10:25), and tells believers that in worship they have come to “the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven” (Hebrews 12:23). Peter gathers Israel's titles from Exodus 19 and applies them to scattered, mostly Gentile believers: “you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), people of whom he can say, “Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God” (1 Peter 2:10). The church is also a flawed body. The letters confront division at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:18), false teaching, favoritism toward the rich in the assembly (James 2:2), and in Revelation seven churches receive praise and rebuke, one of them warned that its lampstand could be removed (Revelation 2:5). The Bible ends with the church complete, the holy city “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,” and the old promise fulfilled: “They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:2-3).

keyTexts.why: God calls Abram to become a great nation through whom all the families of the earth will be blessed. The people of God begins with a promise, and it exists for the sake of the world.
At Sinai the rescued people are named God's treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation. Peter applies these titles to the church (1 Peter 2:9).
God tells Moses to gather the people to hear his words. The day of the assembly at Horeb becomes the pattern for Israel as a qahal, a people called together around God's word.
The promise of a new covenant, with the law written on the heart and sins forgiven. Hebrews 8 applies it to the community Christ has formed.
Jesus promises to build his church on the rock and gives the keys of the kingdom. The founding text, read differently by Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions.
The gathered church exercises discipline and prays with the promise of Christ's presence where two or three gather in his name.
The first church devotes itself to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer, shares goods with the needy, and grows by the Lord's own adding.
The church as the body of Christ, many members baptized by one Spirit into one body, each needing the others.
Christ makes Jew and Gentile one new humanity and builds them into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
Christ loves the church as a husband loves his bride and gives himself for her, to present her holy and without blemish.
The church is God's household and the pillar and foundation of the truth, the community entrusted with guarding and holding up the gospel.
Believers are not to neglect meeting together but to stir one another to love and good works as the Day approaches.
Believers are living stones built into a spiritual house, a royal priesthood and holy nation, once not a people and now the people of God.
The church completed as the new Jerusalem, a bride prepared for her husband, and God dwelling with his people forever.

history:
The earliest Christian writers already reflect on what the church is. Ignatius of Antioch, writing letters on his way to martyrdom in Rome in the early second century, is the first known writer to call the church ‘catholic’, meaning whole or universal, and he tied the unity of each congregation to its bishop. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies, about 180) argued against the Gnostics that the true faith is found in the public teaching handed down in the churches the apostles founded, and he listed the succession of the bishops of Rome as a witness to that continuity. During the persecution under Decius, Cyprian of Carthage wrote On the Unity of the Catholic Church (251), arguing that there is one church, held together by its bishops, and that outside it there is no salvation. The Nicene Creed as expanded at the Council of Constantinople (381) confesses belief in one holy catholic and apostolic church, the four ‘marks’ or ‘notes’ that every major tradition still confesses, and the Apostles' Creed, in its received Western form, confesses the holy catholic church and the communion of saints. In the long controversy with the Donatists, a North African movement that held that a church which tolerated those who had lapsed under persecution was no longer the true church, Augustine (writing from about 400) argued that the church on earth is a mixed body, wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30), and that its holiness comes from Christ, not from the purity of its members.

The Middle Ages saw the church divide and harden. East and West drifted apart over language, authority, and the Nicene Creed's wording about the Spirit, and the mutual excommunications of 1054 are the traditional date of the Great Schism between the Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches. In the West, papal claims reached their height in Boniface VIII's bull Unam Sanctam (1302), which declared submission to the Roman pontiff necessary for salvation. John Wyclif in England (died 1384) and Jan Hus in Bohemia (burned at the Council of Constance in 1415) taught that the true church is the company of the predestined, not identical with the visible hierarchy. The Reformers kept the creedal confession of one church but asked how to recognize it. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 7) defined the church as the assembly of saints in which the gospel is purely taught and the sacraments rightly administered. Luther's On the Councils and the Church (1539) named seven marks by which the church can be known, beginning with the word of God. Calvin (Institutes 4.1, final edition 1559) held the two marks of word and sacraments, called the visible church the mother of believers, and distinguished the church as God sees it, all the elect, from the church as we see it, a mixed company professing faith. The Belgic Confession (1561, Article 29) added church discipline as a third mark. The Anabaptists, in the Schleitheim Confession (1527), and later the Baptists and Congregationalists, insisted that a true church is a gathered company of believers who have personally professed faith, separate from the state. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 25) set out the distinction between the invisible and visible church for English-speaking Presbyterians.

The Roman Catholic response came at the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) and was sharpened at the First Vatican Council (1870), which defined the primacy and infallibility of the pope. The Second Vatican Council's Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, Lumen Gentium (1964), gave new prominence to the biblical image of the church as the people of God, taught that the church of Christ ‘subsists in’ the Catholic Church, and acknowledged that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside its visible structure; its Decree on Ecumenism (1964) called other Christians separated brethren. Among Protestants the nineteenth century brought dispensationalism, associated with John Nelson Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), which sharply distinguished the church from Israel. The twentieth century produced the World Council of Churches (founded in Amsterdam in 1948), the Lausanne Movement among evangelicals (1974), and, above all, the rapid growth of Pentecostal churches and of Christianity in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, where most of the world's Christians now live. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Life Together (1939), drawn from his years leading an underground seminary of the Confessing Church at Finkenwalde, remains a widely read account of what Christian community is. The site's page on the church sets out the Catholic, Reformed, and Baptist understandings of the church, its government, and its sacraments at full strength.

differ.body: Christ founded one visible church and built it on Peter, to whom he gave the keys (Matthew 16:18-19) and the charge to feed his sheep (John 21:15-17). That church continues through bishops in succession from the apostles, united with the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor, who serves as the visible center of unity. The church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, which holds the fullness of the means of salvation, though elements of sanctification and truth are found in other Christian communities, whose members are joined to Catholics by baptism in a real if imperfect communion. The church is not only a gathering of believers but a sacrament of salvation, the body through which Christ continues to teach, sanctify, and govern. Its unity is visible and institutional because the body of Christ is visible, and the church's teaching office guards the faith from dissolving into private opinion.

The church is the continuing life of the risen Christ in his people by the Holy Spirit, known above all in the Eucharist: where the bishop gathers the faithful around the altar, the whole church is present. It is one communion of local churches, each complete, ordered by bishops in apostolic succession who are equals, with honor rather than jurisdiction among the ancient patriarchates. The church has preserved the apostolic faith without addition or subtraction, as defined by the seven ecumenical councils from Nicaea (325) to Nicaea II (787), and truth is guarded not by one office but by the consensus of the whole church, bishops and people together. Defenders stress that this view keeps both the church's visibility and its mystery, and that it refuses the centralization of the West.

The one church is created by the word of God and is recognized wherever the gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly administered, with discipline as a further mark in much Reformed teaching. It exists both as the invisible church, all whom God has elected and joined to Christ in every age, known fully only to him, and as the visible church, the congregations that profess the faith together with their children. The visible church is a true mother to believers yet always a mixed body that needs continual reform by Scripture. Its unity does not depend on a single earthly head or a single line of succession but on the one gospel. Defenders hold that this view takes seriously both Christ's promise to preserve his church and the history of that church's serious errors.

differ.view: Free church and believers' church (Anabaptist, Baptist, Congregational, and many Pentecostal and independent churches)
differ.body: The New Testament church is a gathered company of people who have personally repented, believed, and been baptized, covenanted together under Christ's rule and responsible for one another. The local congregation is the primary visible form of the church; the universal church is the whole company of the redeemed. Membership should be regenerate so far as the church can judge, which is why believers' baptism and church discipline matter so much. The church is distinct from the nation and should never be established by the state or enforced by it. Defenders point to the pattern of Acts, where people heard, believed, were baptized, and were added, and argue that a church mixing believers and unbelievers by birth loses its witness.

errors:
The church has repeatedly rejected the idea that it can be pure in this age by its own effort. The Novatianists in the third century and the Donatists in the fourth drew the boundaries of the true church so tightly around the uncompromised that the church became a society of the morally successful; the wider church answered that the church is holy because Christ is holy and makes it so, not because its members are finished. Jesus' parable of the wheat and the weeds (Matthew 13:24-30) and the frank failures of the churches in Paul's letters and Revelation keep every generation honest. The opposite error treats the church as so identified with Christ that it cannot be judged by his word, or with a nation, an ethnicity, or a political cause, so that belonging to the church becomes the same as belonging to a people or party. Christ's warning to Ephesus that he could remove its lampstand (Revelation 2:5), the Reformers' insistence that the church is always under Scripture, and the witness of Christians who resisted state churches, such as the Confessing Church's Barmen Declaration (1934) against the German Christians who wished to align the church with National Socialism, all stand against that error.

The church has also rejected, with varying words, the idea that a Christian can do without the church. The New Testament knows no believer who is joined to Christ and not to his body; the letters are written to congregations, and their commands (“one another”) cannot be obeyed alone. Equally mistaken is the idea that the church is simply a service provider or a voluntary club of the like-minded, since Paul insists that God places the members in the body as he chooses (1 Corinthians 12:18) and that the rich and poor, Jew and Gentile, slave and free, belong to one another. Finally, the church has rejected contempt for Israel. Paul warns Gentile believers not to boast over the natural branches (Romans 11:18), and the long history of Christian hostility toward Jews, which many churches have formally repented of since the Second World War, is a grievous betrayal of the gospel that the church preaches.
life:
To believe in the church is to accept that faith in Christ is personal but never private. A Christian is someone who has been added to a people, and the ordinary means by which God keeps faith alive (hearing the word read and preached, praying with others, receiving baptism and the Supper, being known, corrected, and forgiven) are all given in the gathered community. Hebrews urges believers not to neglect meeting together precisely because faith grows weak alone. The church is also where a person learns to love people he did not choose: the body of Christ puts together the educated and the uneducated, the old and the young, those of different races and political views, and makes their unity a witness that Christ has done something no human society can do.

The doctrine also frees Christians from both idealism and cynicism about the church. Because the church is Christ's work and not ours, its failures, which are real and sometimes grievous, do not cancel its calling, and because it is a mixed body until the harvest, no congregation should be expected to be the perfect community people long for. For someone wounded by a church, the biblical picture offers both an honest acknowledgment that the church can sin and a reason to hope that Christ has not abandoned his bride. And for every believer, the doctrine points forward: the church we know, gathered in ordinary rooms with ordinary people, is a foretaste of the great assembly from every nation that will stand before God's throne.
questions: The Old Testament calls Israel God's qahal, and the early Christians called themselves the ekklēsia. What does that choice of word suggest about how they understood their relation to Israel and its story?
Paul describes the church as a body, a temple, and a bride. What does each image teach that the others do not, and which of them is most neglected in churches you know?

The traditions differ on whether the church's unity is chiefly visible and institutional or chiefly spiritual and confessional. What do they share, and how should that shape the way Christians of different churches regard one another?
